Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every regular chart density is continuous and strictly positive. The chart integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure independent of the finite charts and subordinate partitions. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. On a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal agrees on chart overlaps and is continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The local graph charts of the smooth boundary form an open cover. Shrinking them gives graph-chart neighborhoods whose coordinate images have compact closure inside Euclidean balls; compactness selects a finite subcover. Rescale each coordinate ball affinely into $(1/4,3/4)^{d-1}$. On each compact chart closure, the map and inverse have bounded derivatives, so the restricted coordinate maps are bi-Lipschitz. Apply [F1] to the finite cover and combine partition functions sharing one chart to obtain nonnegative smooth $\theta_j$ compactly supported in $U_j$, with $\sum_j\theta_j=1$. Since $\sum_j\theta_j^2\ge J^{-1}$, $\psi_j=\theta_j/(\sum_i\theta_i^2)^{1/2}$ is smooth, has the same support, and satisfies $\sum_j\psi_j^2=1$.

For each pair set $\Phi_{jk}(x,y)=(\phi_j(x),\phi_k(y))$ and $\chi_{jk}(x,y)=\psi_j(x)\psi_k(y)$. Define $(Gh)_{jk}(z)=(\chi_{jk}h)(\Phi_{jk}^{-1}z)$ on $\Phi_{jk}(U_j\times U_k)$ and zero elsewhere, and define $(Lv)(x,y)=\sum_{j,k}\chi_{jk}(x,y)v_{jk}(\Phi_{jk}(x,y))$ on the chart pairs, zero outside. These are finite sums. The chart Jacobians and surface-density factors are bounded above and below on compact supports by bi-Lipschitz regularity and [F2]–[F3], with Fubini [F5] for the product chart factors. Thus the pullbacks, zero extensions and smooth multiplications are bounded on $L^2$, so $G$ and $L$ are bounded linear maps.
Substitution in the finite sum gives $(LGh)(x,y)=\sum_{j,k}\chi_{jk}(x,y)^2h(x,y)=(\sum_j\psi_j(x)^2)(\sum_k\psi_k(y)^2)h(x,y)=h(x,y)$ almost everywhere. Thus $LG=I$ as maps on $L^2(M)$.

For smooth $h$, the product and chain rules show that first derivatives of $(Gh)_{jk}$ are bounded chart coefficients times $h$ and its first tangential derivatives. The Jacobian bounds in step 2.1 give $\|Gh\|_{\oplus H^1}\le C\|h\|_{H^1(M)}$ and $\|Lv\|_{H^1(M)}\le C\|v\|_{\oplus H^1}$. Since the weights vanish near patch edges, zero extension remains smooth. Density in the completion definition extends these maps boundedly to $H^1$.

By [F4], $P_N$ is a contraction on the finite direct sum and converges strongly to the identity. The image $G(C)$ is compact by step 2.1. For $\varepsilon>0$, take a finite $\varepsilon/3$-net $v_1,\ldots,v_s$ for $G(C)$ and then take $N$ large enough that $\|P_Nv_i-v_i\|<\varepsilon/3$ for all $i$. For any $v\in G(C)$ choose $v_i$ with $\|v-v_i\|<\varepsilon/3$; contraction gives $\|P_Nv-v\|\le\|P_N(v-v_i)\|+\|P_Nv_i-v_i\|+\|v_i-v\|<\varepsilon$. This proves compact-uniform convergence.

For $w\in H^1(\mathbb T^n)$, weak integration by parts against a character gives $\widehat{\partial_\ell w}(k)=2\pi i k_\ell\widehat w(k)$. Parseval [F4] yields $\|(I-P_N)w\|_2^2=\sum_{\|k\|_\infty>N}|\widehat w(k)|^2\le(2\pi N)^{-2}\sum_k|2\pi k|^2|\widehat w(k)|^2\le(2\pi N)^{-2}\|\nabla w\|_2^2$ for $N\ge1$. Apply this to each component of $Gh$ and use step 3.2. For $N=0$, $\|Gh\|_2\le\|Gh\|_{H^1}\le C\|h\|_{H^1}$; enlarging $C_1$ proves the stated tail estimate.

derivations.claim: Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb R^n$. Since $\sigma$ is not a polynomial, $\sigma^{(m)}$ is not identically zero; choose $b_m$ with $\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)\ne0$. For $h\ne0$ define $R_{m,h}(x):=\frac{1}{\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)h^m}\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^{m-j}\binom mj\sigma(b_m+jh(a\cdot x))$. This is a finite linear combination of permitted units. The repeated-integral formula for the $m$th forward difference gives $R_{m,h}(x)=\frac{(a\cdot x)^m}{\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)}\int_{[0,1]^m}\sigma^{(m)}(b_m+h(a\cdot x)(t_1+\cdots+t_m))\,dt$. Because $a\cdot x$ is bounded on compact $K$ and $\sigma^{(m)}$ is uniformly continuous on a compact interval around $b_m$, $R_{m,h}\to(a\cdot x)^m$ uniformly on $K$ as $h\to0$.

For $m\ge1$ and arbitrary real $x_1,\ldots,x_m$, the polarization identity $x_1\cdots x_m=\frac{1}{2^m m!}\sum_{\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^m}(\prod_{j=1}^m\epsilon_j)(\sum_{j=1}^m\epsilon_jx_j)^m$ expresses each monomial of total degree $m$ in $n$ variables as a finite linear combination of powers of linear forms. Step 1.1 places every such power in the uniform closure of the network family, and that closure is a vector space because finite network sums are represented by concatenating their hidden units. Constants are present through $c_0$. Hence every real polynomial restricted to $K$ belongs to that closure.

The restrictions of real polynomials to $K$ form a unital real function algebra and separate distinct points, since a coordinate function distinguishes any two different points. Compact subsets of Euclidean space are compact Hausdorff, so [L1] makes these polynomial restrictions uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. The network closure contains them by step 2.1 and is therefore all of $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$
and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]), let $\mu\times\nu$ be
their product measure
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]),
let $\overline{\mu\times\nu}$ be its completion
([[def-completed-product-measure]]), and let $k$ be a class in
$L^2(\overline{\mu\times\nu};\mathbb C)$. Write $L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ and
$L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ for the complex $L^2$ spaces of the original measures,
with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ linear in the first variable
([[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. **(representative of finite norm)** there is a
   $(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B)$-measurable representative $k_0$ of $k$ with
   $\int|k_0|^2\,d(\mu\times\nu)<+\infty$, and its norm equals $\|k\|_2$;
2. **(the kernel operator)** for every $f\in L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ the section
   integral $(T_kf)(x):=\int_Yk_0(x,y)f(y)\,d\nu(y)$ converges for
   $\mu$-almost every $x$, agrees almost everywhere with a $\mu$-measurable
   function, and its class in $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ depends only on the classes
   of $f$ and $k$; the resulting map $T_k:L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)\to
   L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is linear and bounded with
   $\|T_k\|\le\|k\|_2$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
   [[def-operator-norm]]);
3. **(exact Hilbert–Schmidt norm)** every Hilbert space admits a Hilbert basis
   under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
   and for every Hilbert basis $E$ of $L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ and every Hilbert
   basis $F$ of $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$,
   $$\sum_{e\in E}\|T_ke\|^2=\sum_{f\in F}\|T_k^*f\|^2=\|k\|_2^2,$$
   the sums being finite-subset suprema
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]); consequently
   $T_k$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every such basis and
   $\|T_k\|_{HS}=\|k\|_2$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]],
   [[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]).

The operator is interpreted through the representative $k_0$ of claim 1, and
claim 2 asserts that no other choice of representative changes the resulting
classes; this is the sense in which a kernel of the completed product defines
an operator on the $L^2$ spaces of the original factors.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

derivations.claim: Let $c_0=|M|^{-1/2}\mathbf1$ and choose a countable orthonormal basis $(c_j)_{j\ge1}$ of $L^2_0(M)$, using [A1] and separability [F1]. Extend $T$ by $\widetilde T c_0=0$ and $\widetilde T c_j=Tc_j$. The Hilbert–Schmidt condition means $\sum_{j\ge1}\|Tc_j\|_2^2<\infty$. Choose measurable representatives and define $\kappa_N(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}(Tc_j)(x)\overline{c_j(y)}$. For $i\ne j$, the summands are orthogonal in $L^2(M\times M)$ because their $y$-factors are orthogonal; Fubini [F3] gives $\|\kappa_N-\kappa_{N'}\|_2^2=\sum_{j=N'+1}^{N}\|Tc_j\|_2^2$ for $N>N'$. Thus $(\kappa_N)$ is Cauchy and converges to $\kappa_T\in L^2(M\times M)$ with $\|\kappa_T\|_2^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\|Tc_j\|_2^2=\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$.

For a finite linear combination $f=\sum_{j=0}^{m}a_jc_j$, orthonormality and the definition of $\kappa_N$ give $\int_M\kappa_N(x,y)f(y)\,dS_y=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(N,m)}a_jTc_j(x)$. Passing to the limit in $N$ gives $\widetilde T f$ in $L^2(M)$. By [F2], the integral operator $K_{\kappa_T}$ is bounded on $L^2(M)$ with norm at most $\|\kappa_T\|_2$; finite linear combinations of the basis are dense, so continuity of $K_{\kappa_T}$ and $\widetilde T$ extends the equality to every $f\in L^2(M)$.

Since $\widetilde T c_0=0$, step 2.1 with $f=c_0$ yields $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_y=0$ for almost every $x$. Since the range of $\widetilde T$ lies in $L^2_0(M)$, for every $f\in L^2(M)$ Fubini gives $0=\int_M\widetilde T f(x)\,dS_x=\int_M f(y)(\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_x)\,dS_y$. The inner section is in $L^2(M)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and [F3]; its pairing with every $f$ vanishes, so it is zero almost everywhere. This proves the two zero-mean properties.

If $\kappa'$ is another $L^2$ kernel for $\widetilde T$, let $q=\kappa_T-\kappa'$. For every pair of basis vectors $c_i,c_j$, the coefficient $\int_{M\times M}q(x,y)c_j(y)\overline{c_i(x)}\,dS_xdS_y$ is zero because both kernels represent the same operator. If $q$ is orthogonal to all products $c_i(x)\overline{c_j(y)}$, Fubini makes each section coefficient $\int_Mq(x,y)\overline{c_j(y)}dS_y$ vanish for almost every $x$; Countable Choice gives one conull set for all $j$, and completeness of $(c_j)$ then gives $q(x,\cdot)=0$ there. Hence $q=0$ in $L^2(M\times M)$, proving uniqueness.

The kernel is unique, has the prescribed zero-mean convention, and has the exact norm in step 1.1. This establishes the claimed kernel representation without relying on the reverse implication of [F2].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\sigma\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ be globally Lipschitz and nonpolynomial. Let $T:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^a)\to L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)$ be continuous, let $C$ be a compact subset of the input space, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Then a finite Fourier neural operator on $\mathbb T^n$, with finitely many channels and layers, finite Fourier multipliers, continuous periodic bias functions, coordinatewise activation $\sigma$, and a final pointwise affine output map, satisfies
$$\sup_{f\in C}\|T(f)-\Phi(f)\|_{L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon.$$

Let $M\subset\mathbb R^{d_a}$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension $n\ge d$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a bounded domain, and let $\sigma\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ be globally Lipschitz and nonpolynomial. Fix finite input and output channel dimensions. A generalized Fourier neural operator is a map $\Psi:L^2(M;\mathbb R^{d_{in}})\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_{out}})$ of the form
$$\Psi=Q\circ R\circ F\circ L_L\circ\cdots\circ L_1\circ E\circ S.$$
Here $S$ is a pointwise finite-dimensional affine network, $S(h)(x)=s(x,h(x))$; $E$ is a continuous linear chart-lifting map from manifold functions to multichannel functions on $\mathbb T^n$; each $L_\ell$ acts on periodic channel fields by a fixed matrix channel map plus a continuous periodic channel bias $b_\ell(x)$ and a finite Fourier-multiplier convolution, followed coordinatewise by $\sigma$; $F:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^{c})\to L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^{r})$ is a continuous linear dimension-reduction layer
$$ (Fv)(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\int_{\mathbb T^{n-d}}K(z)v(x_1,\ldots,x_d,z)\,dz,$$
with a finite-dimensional matrix kernel $K$; $R$ is restriction of periodic fields to $\Omega$; and $Q$ is a pointwise finite-dimensional output network. For the EIT boundary manifold $M=\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega$, the chart-lifting map $E$ may be taken to be the map $G$ of the chart-lifting lemma, with its finite chart-pair array treated as input channels. The finite Fourier multiplier at a layer is $\widehat{\mathcal K v}(k)=R_k\widehat v(k)$ for finitely many $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, with real-valued outputs enforced by conjugate-symmetric coefficients. When $n=d$, $F$ is the identity layer.

This is an architecture definition only. It asserts no approximation, training, statistical, discretization, or computational-cost guarantee.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be an open domain whose closure is compact and contained in $\Omega$. Fix real parameters $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is covered by finitely many $C^1$ graph charts. Give $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ its Sobolev norm, let $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ have the finite-chart Slobodeckij norm. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with its quotient norm. The trace induces a bounded linear bijection $\overline T:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with bounded inverse, so these two norms are equivalent under the induced identification. The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every regular chart density is continuous and strictly positive. The chart integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure independent of the finite charts and subordinate partitions. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. On a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal agrees on chart overlaps and is continuous.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $V=\{v\in H^1(\Omega):\int_\Omega v\,dx=0\}$, a closed Hilbert subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$. By [F2], $\|v\|_{H^1}\le C_0\|
abla v\|_2$ on $V$, where $C_0=(1+C^2)^{1/2}$. By [F1], the form $a_\gamma(u,v)=\int_\Omega\gamma
abla u\cdot\overline{
abla v}$ is bounded on $V$ and $a_\gamma(v,v)\ge m\|
abla v\|_2^2\ge mC_0^{-2}\|v\|_{H^1}^2$. Thus it is bounded and coercive on $V$.

Define $\ell_F(v)=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])$ for $v\in V$. By [F3], the quotient trace norm of $[\operatorname{Tr}v]$ is at most $C_1\|v\|_{H^1}$, so $|\ell_F(v)|\le C_1\|F\|\|v\|_{H^1}$; hence $\ell_F$ is bounded on $V$. Applying [F4] to step 1.1 gives a unique $u_0\in V$ with $a_\gamma(u_0,v)=\ell_F(v)$ for every $v\in V$.

For arbitrary $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ write $v=v_0+c$ with $v_0=v-v_\Omega\in V$ and $c=v_\Omega$. Gradients are unchanged by adding $c$, and $F$ acts on the trace quotient by constants, so the equation for $u_0$ on $V$ implies it for every $v\in H^1$. If $u_1$ is another solution class, subtract its volume mean to obtain $w\in V$ with $a_\gamma(w,v)=0$ for all $v\in V$; setting $v=w$ and using coercivity from step 1.1 gives $w=0$. Thus the solution is unique modulo constants.

The estimate in [F4] and step 2.1 give $\|u_0\|_{H^1}\le C_0^2C_1m^{-1}\|F\|$. The bounded trace map [F3] therefore makes the solution class in $\dot{\mathcal D}$ a bounded linear function of $F$. By [F5], the compact smooth boundary has finite positive surface measure. Subtracting the surface mean of $\operatorname{Tr}u_0$ selects one representative with boundary mean zero; this constant shift preserves the weak equation and is the only such shift. For mean-zero $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$, Cauchy–Schwarz and the trace bound show $F_f$ is continuous, and its zero mean makes it independent of the representative modulo constants. This proves the final assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ be a real conductivity. Write $M=\partial\Omega$, let $dS$ be surface measure, and set
$$L^2_0(M)=\left\{f\in L^2(M):\int_M f\,dS=0\right\},\qquad P_0f=f-|M|^{-1}\int_Mf\,dS.$$
The mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ sends $f$ to the mean-zero boundary trace of the weak solution of $\nabla\cdot(\gamma\nabla u)=0$ with outward conormal flux $f$, as defined by the weak Neumann problem. Let $-\Delta_M$ be the nonnegative Laplace–Beltrami operator on the compact boundary manifold, with eigenpairs $(e_j,\lambda_j)$ on $L^2_0(M)$ from its spectral resolution. For $\tau=1/2$ when $d=2$ and any fixed $\tau>0$ when $d\ge3$, put
$$r_d:=\frac{d-1}{2}-1+\tau,\qquad C_M^{r_d/2}e_j=(1+\lambda_j)^{-r_d/2}e_j.$$
The smoothed observation is the bounded operator $A_\gamma:=\mathscr R_\gamma C_M^{r_d/2}:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$. Its extension to all of $L^2(M)$ is $\widetilde A_\gamma f=\iota_0A_\gamma(P_0f)$, where $\iota_0:L^2_0(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is inclusion. Thus its integral kernel, when it exists in $L^2(M\times M)$, is fixed to have zero mean in each variable. No assertion of a kernel's existence or Hilbert–Schmidt regularity is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $M=\partial\Omega$ be the compact smooth boundary in the boundary spectral setting, let $P_0$ be projection onto $L^2_0(M)$, and let $T:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ be Hilbert–Schmidt. Extend $T$ to $\widetilde T:L^2(M)\to L^2(M)$ by $\widetilde T=\iota_0TP_0$, where $\iota_0$ is inclusion. Then there is a unique $\kappa_T\in L^2(M\times M)$ such that
$$\widetilde T f(x)=\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)f(y)\,dS_y\quad\text{for almost every }x\text{ and every }f\in L^2(M),$$
and
$$\|\kappa_T\|_{L^2(M\times M)}=\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.$$
The kernel has zero mean in each variable: $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_y=0$ for almost every $x$, and $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_x=0$ for almost every $y$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$
and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]), let $\mu\times\nu$ be
their product measure
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]),
let $\overline{\mu\times\nu}$ be its completion
([[def-completed-product-measure]]), and let $k$ be a class in
$L^2(\overline{\mu\times\nu};\mathbb C)$. Write $L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ and
$L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ for the complex $L^2$ spaces of the original measures,
with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ linear in the first variable
([[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. **(representative of finite norm)** there is a
   $(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B)$-measurable representative $k_0$ of $k$ with
   $\int|k_0|^2\,d(\mu\times\nu)<+\infty$, and its norm equals $\|k\|_2$;
2. **(the kernel operator)** for every $f\in L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ the section
   integral $(T_kf)(x):=\int_Yk_0(x,y)f(y)\,d\nu(y)$ converges for
   $\mu$-almost every $x$, agrees almost everywhere with a $\mu$-measurable
   function, and its class in $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ depends only on the classes
   of $f$ and $k$; the resulting map $T_k:L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)\to
   L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is linear and bounded with
   $\|T_k\|\le\|k\|_2$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
   [[def-operator-norm]]);

([[def-compact-linear-operator]],

[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues

   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For each fixed integer $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<1$, and let $\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)$. Set
$$\delta:=\|\dot{\Lambda}_\gamma-\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1,(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*)}.$$
There exist constants $C>0$, $\rho>0$ and $t_0\in(0,1)$, depending only on $d,\alpha,\Omega,\Omega',m,M,R$, such that
$$\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\,\omega(\delta),\qquad \omega(0):=0,\qquad \omega(t):=\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{t,t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(t>0).$$
Here $X_d(R)$ is the BV class when $d=2$ and the bounded $C^{1,\alpha}$ class when $d\ge3$, and $\dot\Lambda_\gamma$ is the induced weak conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on the trace quotient by constants.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $I$ be any set, let $x\in H_1$, and let $(x_i)_{i\in I}\subset H_1$ and $(y_i)_{i\in I}\subset H_2$. Let $\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\omega(0)=0$. If
$$\|y_i-y_j\|\le\omega(\|x_i-x_j\|)\qquad(i,j\in I),$$
then
$$\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline B\bigl(y_i,\omega(\|x_i-x\|)\bigr)\ne\varnothing.$$
The intersection over an empty index set means all of $H_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$. Write $M=\partial\Omega$, $n=d-1$, and let $A_\gamma$ and $\widetilde A_\gamma$ be the mean-zero smoothed NtD observation and its extension from the preceding definition. Then $\widetilde A_\gamma$ is Hilbert–Schmidt on $L^2(M)$ and has a unique zero-mean-in-each-variable kernel $\kappa_\gamma\in L^2(M\times M)$, with
$$\|\kappa_\gamma\|_{L^2(M\times M)}=\|\widetilde A_\gamma\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.$$
The Hilbert–Schmidt norms are uniformly bounded over $X_d(R)$. Moreover, there is $C<\infty$, depending only on the fixed class and domain, such that
$$\|\dot\Lambda_\gamma-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\dot{\mathcal D},\dot{\mathcal D}^{*})}\le C\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_{L^2(M\times M)}^{1/2}\qquad(\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(P, \le)$ be a
nonempty poset in which **every chain has an upper bound**. Then $P$ has a
maximal element ([[def-maximal-element]]).

Note the hypothesis asks only for an upper bound, not a least upper bound, and
the conclusion asserts only that a maximal element exists, never that a greatest
one does.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Every nonempty chain has as upper bound the union of its graphs: every two of its domain points occur together in one member of the chain, so the same modulus inequality holds for their union. For the EIT application first arrange $t_0\le e^{-(\rho+1)}$. If the original IP-45 constants have a larger cutoff, decrease it and enlarge $C_0$ if needed: the uniform class diameter is at most $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$, so taking $C_0\ge2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$ covers all DN distances above the new cutoff, while increasing $C_0$ preserves the old small-distance estimate. For $0<s<(t_0/C_1)^2$, put $L(s)=\log(1/(C_1\sqrt{s}))$ and $\varphi(s)=C_0L(s)^{-\rho}$. Then $\varphi'(s)=C_0\rho/(2sL(s)^{\rho+1})>0$ and $\varphi''(s)=C_0\rho[\rho+1-2L(s)]/(4s^2L(s)^{\rho+2})\le0$. At the cutoff it joins continuously to a constant and its derivative drops to zero; at zero it tends to zero. Thus the displayed $\omega_\star$ is continuous, nondecreasing and concave on the entire nonnegative half-line.

This also covers $B=\varnothing$, since [F2]'s empty intersection is $H_2$, which contains zero. Thus $B=H_1$ and $\widetilde g=h$ proves the full same-modulus extension theorem for arbitrary real Hilbert spaces and arbitrary subsets.

$$L^2_0(M)=\left\{f\in L^2(M):\int_M f\,dS=0\right\},\qquad P_0f=f-|M|^{-1}\int_Mf\,dS.$$
The mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ sends $f$ to the mean-zero boundary trace of the weak solution of $\nabla\cdot(\gamma\nabla u)=0$ with outward conormal flux $f$, as defined by the weak Neumann problem. Let $-\Delta_M$ be the nonnegative Laplace–Beltrami operator on the compact boundary manifold, with eigenpairs $(e_j,\lambda_j)$ on $L^2_0(M)$ from its spectral resolution. For $\tau=1/2$ when $d=2$ and any fixed $\tau>0$ when $d\ge3$, put
$$r_d:=\frac{d-1}{2}-1+\tau,\qquad C_M^{r_d/2}e_j=(1+\lambda_j)^{-r_d/2}e_j.$$
The smoothed observation is the bounded operator $A_\gamma:=\mathscr R_\gamma C_M^{r_d/2}:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$. Its extension to all of $L^2(M)$ is $\widetilde A_\gamma f=\iota_0A_\gamma(P_0f)$, where $\iota_0:L^2_0(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is inclusion. Thus its integral kernel, when it exists in $L^2(M\times M)$, is fixed to have zero mean in each variable. No assertion of a kernel's existence or Hilbert–Schmidt regularity is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $A\subseteq H_1$, and let $g:A\to H_2$. If a continuous, nondecreasing, concave function $\omega_\star:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ satisfies $\omega_\star(0)=0$ and
$$\|g(x)-g(y)\|_{H_2}\le\omega_\star(\|x-y\|_{H_1})\qquad(x,y\in A),$$
then the Hilbert-valued same-modulus extension theorem asserts that there is $\widetilde g:H_1\to H_2$ extending $g$ and satisfying the same inequality for every $x,y\in H_1$.

$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$

A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be the Hilbert transform of
[[cor-hilbert-transform-is-an-ltwo-isometry-and-squares-to-minus-identity|the line]]
and, for $1\le j\le n$, let $R_j$ be the Riesz transform of
[[def-riesz-transforms-on-euclidean-space]]. Then $H$ and each $R_j$ are
Calderon-Zygmund operators with the kernels $k(x)=1/(\pi x)$ and
$K_j(x)=c_nx_j/|x|^{n+1}$: they are $L^2$-bounded with norm at most $1$, and
for every compactly supported $f\in L^2$ and almost every
$x\notin\operatorname{supp}f$ one has $Tf(x)=\int k(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ with the
kernel of $T$. Moreover both kernels are standard $1$-Holder Calderon-Zygmund
kernels with the published constants ($A_2'=2/\pi$ and
$C_n=c_n2^{n+1}(3n+4)$, respectively).

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $T$ be a Calderón–Zygmund operator with kernel constants $A_1,A_2$ and $L^2$
norm $B$. Then for every $1<p<\infty$, $T$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator
on $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$$\|Tf\|_p\le C_{n,p}(A_2+B)\max\bigl(p,(p-1)^{-1}\bigr)\|f\|_p,$$
where $C_{n,p}$ depends only on $n$ and $p$. In fact $C_{n,p}$ may be chosen to be a dimensional constant $C_n$ independent of $p$.

Assume countable choice. Work with complex-valued $L^p$ spaces and a complex-linear operator.
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be measure spaces. Let
$1\le p_0,p_1<\infty$, let $1<q_0,q_1<\infty$, let $0<\theta<1$, and define
$$\frac1{p_\theta}:=\frac{1-\theta}{p_0}+\frac{\theta}{p_1}, \qquad \frac1{q_\theta}:=\frac{1-\theta}{q_0}+\frac{\theta}{q_1},$$

Suppose $T$ is a complex-linear map from the almost-everywhere classes of complex finite simple functions with finite-measure nonzero set on $X$ to measurable complex almost-everywhere classes on $Y$, and suppose $M_0,M_1\ge0$ satisfy
$$\|Tf\|_{q_0}\le M_0\|f\|_{p_0}, \qquad \|Tf\|_{q_1}\le M_1\|f\|_{p_1}$$
for every such $f$. Then $T$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear operator
$$\widetilde T:L^{p_\theta}(\mu;\mathbb C)\to L^{q_\theta}(\nu;\mathbb C)$$
satisfying
$$\|\widetilde T f\|_{q_\theta}\le M_0^{1-\theta}M_1^\theta\|f\|_{p_\theta} \qquad(f\in L^{p_\theta}(\mu)).$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain with a bounded extension operator $E$, and let $1\le p<n$, $p\le q\le p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously:
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, open, bounded and a $W^{1,p}$-extension domain for every $p\in(n/2,n)$ (the extension operator may depend on $p$). For every $1\le q<\infty$ there is $C(n,q,\Omega)$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,n}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,n}(\Omega;\mathbb K));$$
that is, $W^{1,n}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously for every finite $q$. The constant necessarily blows up as $q\to\infty$, so no $L^\infty$ bound is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^1$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal D(\Omega)=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the trace quotient and write $\dot{\mathcal D}=\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$. For each $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$ there is a unique weak solution class $[u]\in H^1(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}\,dx=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The resulting solution operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}\to\dot{\mathcal D}$ is bounded. Its unique representative whose boundary trace has surface mean zero solves the same weak equation. In particular, for $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$ with $\int_{\partial\Omega}f\,dS=0$, the functional $F_f([g])=\int_{\partial\Omega}f\overline g\,dS$ is admissible and defines the mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map on mean-zero $L^2$ fluxes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $1 \le p,q,r \le \infty$ satisfy

$$ \frac1r = \frac1p + \frac1q - 1. $$

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then the
convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. With $\omega_{n-1}=|S^{n-1}|>0$ in the published chart/polar convention, set $\Phi(x)=|x|^{2-n}/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ for $n\ge3$ and $\Phi(x)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x|$ for $n=2$, $x\ne0$. Extend it as a locally integrable function at the pole. The one-dimensional analogue is $-\tfrac12|x|$; the subsequent $n\ge2$ Green theory does not silently include it.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge2$. The locally integrable kernel $\Phi$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]] defines a regular distribution $T_\Phi\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ and satisfies $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$. For every $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the regular distribution associated with $x\mapsto\Phi(x-y)$ satisfies $-\Delta_x T_{\Phi(\cdot-y)}=\delta_y$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^1$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal D(\Omega)=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the trace quotient and write $\dot{\mathcal D}=\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$. For each $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$ there is a unique weak solution class $[u]\in H^1(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}\,dx=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The resulting solution operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}\to\dot{\mathcal D}$ is bounded. Its unique representative whose boundary trace has surface mean zero solves the same weak equation. In particular, for $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$ with $\int_{\partial\Omega}f\,dS=0$, the functional $F_f([g])=\int_{\partial\Omega}f\overline g\,dS$ is admissible and defines the mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map on mean-zero $L^2$ fluxes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is covered by finitely many $C^1$ graph charts. Give $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ its Sobolev norm, let $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ have the finite-chart Slobodeckij norm. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with its quotient norm. The trace induces a bounded linear bijection $\overline T:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with bounded inverse, so these two norms are equivalent under the induced identification. The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$;
write $\delta_hu=(\delta_h^1u,\dots,\delta_h^nu)$ and
$Du=(D_1u,\dots,D_nu)$ for the difference-quotient and gradient vectors, with
$$\|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|\delta_h^iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega')},\qquad \|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
(1) If $1\le p\le\infty$ and $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then for every
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)$ and every coordinate
direction $i$,
$$\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le n^{|1/p-1/2|}\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
At $p=2$ the vector estimate has constant one. The coordinate bound also
holds on any open $U\subseteq\Omega$ for a fixed $i,h$ for which every
segment $[x,x+he_i]$, $x\in U$, stays in $\Omega$; compact containment
is unnecessary. In particular, $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(H)}\le
\|D_iu\|_{L^p(H)}$ for tangential directions on a half-space $H$.
(2) Conversely, if $1<p<\infty$, $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and there is $C$
with $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$ for every coordinate $i$ and all
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)/2$, then
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega')$ with $D_iu\in L^p(\Omega')$,
$\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$, and
$\delta_h^iu\rightharpoonup D_iu$ weakly in $L^p(\Omega')$ as $h\to0$.
For $1\le p<\infty$, tangential quotients on $H$ also converge strongly:
$\delta_h^iu\to D_iu$ in $L^p(H)$ as $h\to0$.
Both parts are identities of classes and hold without any regularity of
$\partial\Omega$. At $p=1$ the converse in (2) is deliberately not asserted;
the companion remark records why only a measure derivative survives there.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $k\ge0$, and let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$,
$b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, all derivatives bounded by
constants $M_\ell$; let $f\in H^k_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and let
$u\in H^1(\Omega)$ be a local weak solution of $Lu=f$
([[def-local-weak-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]). Then
$u\in H^{k+2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and for all open sets
$\Omega'\Subset\Omega''\Subset\Omega$ there is
$C=C(n,\theta,k,M_0,\dots,M_{k+1},\Omega',\Omega'')$ with
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega')}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega'')}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega'')}\big).$$
The gain is exactly two derivatives; the coefficient regularity required is
one order above the data order. For $k=0$ the theorem reduces to
[[thm-interior-h-two-regularity-for-divergence-form-equations]]. The
scaffold wrote $\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ on the right-hand
side, which is ill-posed for locally Sobolev data on an unbounded $\Omega$;
the nested formulation is the well-posed local statement.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be closed and convex with $x\in H$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\operatorname{Re}\langle x-p,\ y-p\rangle\le0 \qquad \text{for every } y\in C .$$

In particular, for the nearest point the inequality holds, and conversely any $p\in C$ satisfying the inequality is nearest.
